clinicalPearls: A congenital anomaly in which the urethral opening lies on the ventral aspect of the penis rather than at the tip, resulting from incomplete tubularisation of the urethral plate
The severity spectrum runs from a distal (glanular or coronal) meatus to more proximal penoscrotal or perineal positions, the latter being functionally more significant
It is commonly accompanied by ventral penile curvature (chordee) and a dorsally hooded, incompletely formed prepuce
Severe or proximal hypospadias, particularly when combined with cryptorchidism or a bifid scrotum, should prompt evaluation for a disorder of sex development
Circumcision should be avoided in affected infants because the foreskin is often needed as tissue for surgical reconstruction
Surgical repair aims to reposition the meatus, straighten the penis, and achieve a normal cosmetic and functional result, usually undertaken in early childhood
Isolated distal hypospadias in an otherwise normally virilised boy generally does not require an extensive endocrine workup
reference.pathophysiology: During male genital development, androgen-driven fusion of the urethral folds progresses from proximal to distal to form the penile urethra and close the ventral shaft. Hypospadias results when this tubularisation is incomplete, leaving the urethral meatus proximal to its normal position and often accompanied by a ventral tethering of tissue (chordee) and a defect in foreskin formation. The defect reflects inadequate or mistimed androgen action, or disturbance of the developmental signalling that guides urethral closure. When hypospadias is proximal and severe or occurs with undescended testes, it more often signals a broader disturbance of sexual differentiation, whereas isolated distal disease usually represents a localised developmental anomaly.
additionalDifferentials: Disorder of sex development, including partial androgen insensitivity and defects of testosterone or dihydrotestosterone synthesis
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia causing atypical genitalia
Epispadias (dorsally placed meatus) as part of the exstrophy-epispadias spectrum
Buried or webbed penis with an apparently displaced meatus
additionalInvestigations: Thorough genital examination to define meatal position, degree of chordee, and scrotal and testicular findings
Karyotype and disorder-of-sex-development evaluation in proximal or severe cases or with associated cryptorchidism
Serum electrolytes and 17-hydroxyprogesterone to exclude congenital adrenal hyperplasia where indicated
LH, FSH, testosterone, and anti-Müllerian hormone to assess gonadal function in complex cases
hCG stimulation test to evaluate testicular androgen production when a synthetic defect is suspected
Pelvic ultrasound to assess internal genital structures in ambiguous presentations
redFlags: Proximal hypospadias with unilateral or bilateral cryptorchidism, suggesting a disorder of sex development requiring urgent assessment
Any genital ambiguity or a bifid scrotum accompanying the hypospadias
Features suggestive of salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia in a virilised infant
Impaired urinary stream or difficulty voiding related to meatal position
reference.prognosis: Distal hypospadias has an excellent outcome after repair, with good cosmetic and functional results; more proximal forms may require staged or complex reconstruction and carry a higher rate of complications such as fistula or stricture, but most children ultimately achieve satisfactory urinary and sexual function.
pitfalls: Permitting neonatal circumcision, thereby removing foreskin tissue that is valuable for later repair
Failing to evaluate proximal hypospadias with cryptorchidism as a possible disorder of sex development
Overlooking congenital adrenal hyperplasia in an infant with atypical genitalia and its salt-wasting risk
Missing associated chordee, which must be corrected to achieve a straight, functional penis
Subjecting isolated distal hypospadias to an unnecessarily extensive endocrine investigation
management: Undertake surgical repair (urethroplasty) to reposition the meatus, with orthoplasty to correct chordee and reconstruction using preputial or oral mucosal tissue, usually in early childhood
Avoid circumcision so the foreskin is preserved as reconstructive tissue
For proximal or severe disease, plan staged reconstruction and consider preoperative topical or parenteral androgen stimulation to enlarge the phallus
Evaluate proximal, severe or cryptorchidism-associated cases for a disorder of sex development, including karyotype and endocrine assessment, before surgery
Monitor postoperatively for urethrocutaneous fistula, meatal stenosis and urethral stricture
Manage within a paediatric urology and endocrinology multidisciplinary team, involving clinical genetics where a disorder of sex development is identified
